The Argentine giant tegu, Salvator merianae, exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in body size, a trait common among large-bodied teiid lizards. Adult females attain a maximum total length of 91 centimeters [Li = 91 centimeters], a figure consistently documented in field studies across their Argentine range. Males, by contrast, regularly achieve a significantly larger ultimate length of 140 centimeters [Li = 140 centimeters], reflecting the selective pressures associated with intrasexual competition for territories and nesting sites. This divergence in size is established during the prolonged juvenile and sub-adult growth phase, which in this species spans approximately eight months at an average body temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. Neonates of this species emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs at a remarkably modest size, with a typical wet weight at birth of 10 grams [Wwb = 10 grams]. This low initial mass belies the extraordinary growth capacity that will be realized over the subsequent months of development. The incubation period, which proceeds at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], lasts approximately 64 days [ab = approximately 64 days] before the hatchlings begin to pip through the shell using their egg caruncle. During this developmental interval, the embryos rely entirely on the substantial yolk reserves deposited in the fertilized ovum, transitioning to exogenous feeding only after the yolk-sac larva stage is complete. The thermal sensitivity of this incubation period is notable; at slightly higher temperatures typical of sun-exposed nest sites, development can be accelerated considerably, though 25 °C [T = 25 °C] represents a commonly measured mean in the southern portions of their distribution where soils are cooler throughout the breeding season.

Reproductive output in Salvator merianae is substantial for a lizard of its size, reflecting a life-history strategy that balances high fecundity with extended parental investment at the nest. At a sustained body temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], females produce 18 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 18 eggs per clutch], laying two clutches each year [F_R_i = two clutches each year]. This annual reproductive investment is constrained by the need to accumulate sufficient body reserves, as females typically fast during the nesting period while guarding their eggs. The attainment of puberty marks a critical threshold in this species' life cycle; individuals must reach a wet weight at puberty of 1500 grams [Wwp = 1500 grams] before gonadal activation and the onset of reproductive activity can occur. This mass-based trigger for maturation ensures that females are large enough to produce and energetically support a full clutch without compromising their own somatic condition.

The ultimate body mass achieved by fully grown adults places S. merianae among the largest of the teiid lizards. Adult females and males can attain a maximum recorded wet weight of 7 kilograms [Wwi = 7 kilograms], though individuals exceeding 6 kilograms are more commonly documented in populations with access to high-quality habitats. This substantial adult mass is supported by a relatively slow metabolic rate consistent with the species' opportunistic, energy-conserving foraging strategy. Field studies conducted in the open grasslands of central Argentina indicate that maximum longevity under natural conditions is approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years] when individuals are maintained at a mean annual body temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This lifespan is remarkable for a terrestrial reptile and is comparable to that of much larger chelonians, suggesting that the species has evolved effective mechanisms for mitigating oxidative stress and cellular senescence over extended periods.

The ecological role of S. merianae as both predator and prey is mediated by its large body size and its capacity for thermoregulatory precision. Juveniles face high predation pressure from raptors and snakes, and their survival to the wet weight at puberty of 1.5 kilograms [Wwp = 1.5 kilograms] is a critical demographic bottleneck. Females investing in reproduction at 30 °C [T = 30 °C] produce two clutches annually [F_R_i = two clutches annually] that range from 18 to 25 eggs each [N_R_i = 18 to 25 eggs each], a strategy that compensates for relatively high rates of nest predation by mammalian mesopredators. The species' exceptional longevity of 7300 days [am = 7300 days] under optimal captive conditions underscores its slow life-history pace relative to other large sauropsids at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].
